control_ladder.note_beginner: Where pea viruses turn up in your area, start at the seed rack. Cascadia and Sugar Sprint are snap varieties that resist those viruses. The resistance is to the virus rather than to the aphid itself, so you may still see the insects.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cascadia and Sugar Sprint carry virus resistance, worth choosing where pea viruses are a known local problem. It addresses the transmission outcome, not the aphid population, so pair it with the steps below.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lay reflective mulch, a silvery plastic or foil sheet, on the soil while the plants are still small. It confuses aphids looking for somewhere to land and cuts down the viruses they carry in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch disorients incoming aphids, reducing both feeding and the virus spread that is the real risk here. Lay it early, while the canopy is still open enough for the soil to show.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the weeds and clover near the bed. Aphids shelter and build up in them before moving across onto your peas.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Nearby weeds and clover act as a reservoir. Clearing them before sowing and holding the row edges clean through the season cuts the source population that colonizes the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Too much nitrogen pushes soft, lush new growth, which is the growth aphids prefer.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Excess nitrogen produces the succulent tissue pea aphid favors. Feeding restraint makes the crop a poorer host rather than treating an infestation after it forms.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Knock the colonies off with a strong jet of water from the hose. Do this as soon as you spot them, while there are only a few clusters on the tips.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful water spray dislodges colonies from growing tips, flower stalks and leaf undersides. Most useful while numbers are low, which is also when the virus risk is easiest to blunt.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the helpful insects a chance to work. Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which lay their eggs inside aphids, usually bring the numbers down on their own.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Lady beetles, lacewings and parasitoid wasps generally catch up with pea aphid without intervention. The lag is widest in cool spring and fall weather, when the aphid reproduces faster than they build.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the colonies keep building, insecticidal soap kills the aphids it touches directly, so wet the growing tips and the undersides of leaves where they cluster. Start while numbers are still low.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is contact-only, so coverage of tips and leaf undersides governs the result. Begin at the first colonies rather than waiting for curling or yellowing, since transmission runs ahead of visible damage.

control_ladder.note_beginner: After harvest, pull the spent pea plants and destroy them instead of leaving them in the bed. The adult beetles spend the winter in that trash.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Destroying pea residue after harvest strips the overwintering shelter adults use. With a single generation a year, removing that refuge acts directly on next spring's pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow next year's peas in a different part of the garden, away from the bed that just carried them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rotating off last year's pea ground puts distance between emerging adults and the new crop. Host range is peas alone, so a bed of anything else offers them nothing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where this beetle is established, sowing early helps. If the pods finish filling before the adults are at their busiest, the crop can slip past the worst of it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: An early sowing that completes pod fill ahead of peak adult activity escapes the heaviest egg-laying. Adults move in at bloom, so bloom through pod fill is the stretch that has to be missed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Watch the plants while they are flowering, which is when the beetles arrive to lay eggs, and pick off the ones you find on the blossoms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Scout blossoms through bloom, the egg-laying window, and remove adults by hand. Practical at home-patch scale, and it cuts the eggs placed on young pods.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put a light row cover over the planting once the peas start to flower. It keeps the beetles off the young pods so they have nowhere to lay.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover applied at flowering excludes adults through the egg-laying window, the narrow period that decides how many larvae end up developing inside the seeds.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear the weeds and tall grass around the bed before you sow. That cover is where the moths lay, so taking it away means fewer caterpillars to deal with later.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy and grassy cover supplies the egg-laying sites. Clearing it before sowing and keeping the row edges clean all season shrinks the pool that moves into the planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Turn the soil in the bed a couple of weeks before you plant. It brings the caterpillars already living there up to the surface, where they dry out.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Working the bed roughly two weeks ahead of sowing exposes resident larvae and dries them out before emergence, which is the stage that suffers most.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go out in the evening or first thing in the morning and pick the caterpillars off. When you find a toppled seedling, scratch around in the soil right beside it and you will usually turn up the cutworm, curled tight.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both groups feed at night and shelter in soil or debris by day, so scout at dusk or first light. A toppled seedling marks the spot, with the cutworm curled in the soil alongside it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ring each young seedling with a collar of cardboard or foil pushed a little way into the soil. It blocks cutworms from reaching the stem.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A cardboard or foil collar set at the soil line physically blocks cutworms during establishment. Worth the labor only over the seedling stage they target.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cover the young seedlings with a light row cover. It keeps the egg-laying moths off the planting, and it is worth doing if these caterpillars show up most years where you garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Row cover over emerging seedlings denies the moths a place to lay and protects the vulnerable stage. Reserve it for beds with a local history of this problem.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For armyworms already chewing the leaves, Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis, a bacterium that affects caterpillars) is the spray. It works on young ones, so treat while they are small.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bt covers the foliage-feeding armyworm half of this pair and is most effective on young larvae. The cutworm half is addressed by the collar rung above rather than by a foliar application.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull the weeds near the bed, since thrips shelter in them and move across into the peas from there.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Weedy hosts around the planting carry thrips populations. Clearing them and keeping the edges clean limits what moves in during the warm, dry stretch late in the pea season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Reflective mulch, a silvery sheet laid on the soil, confuses them on the way in and helps with the viruses they can carry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Reflective mulch disorients incoming thrips and reduces virus spread. Laid early, while the canopy is still open enough for the soil to show.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Peas usually shrug off light thrips damage, so often you need do nothing at all. If numbers climb, a strong jet of water from the hose knocks them back.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Light feeding is generally outgrown untreated. Where numbers climb, a forceful water spray reduces them, and most home pea crops finish before pressure peaks.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Helpful insects such as minute pirate bugs and lacewings feed on thrips and often keep them in check for you.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Minute pirate bugs and lacewings contribute real suppression. Conserving them is the better trade on a low-severity problem the crop usually outruns.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If they keep building, insecticidal soap reduces them on contact, so wet the leaves and pods where you can see the silvery scarring.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap works only where it lands, so coverage governs the result. Hold it for the uncommon case where feeding is distorting new growth or scarring pods, and keep the crop watered, since drought-stressed vines are more prone.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here. A resistant variety is the best defense against this one, and the snap peas give you choices: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint each resist powdery mildew.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistance is the highest-leverage step against a disease that moves fast once established and is difficult to arrest late. Three snap cultivars offer it: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the plants room and put up a trellis so air moves through the vines instead of sitting still inside a tangle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spacing and a trellis hold the canopy open through the season. This is a planting-time decision and the cheapest one on the ladder.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off the worst-hit leaves as soon as you notice the powdery patches. Catching it at the first spots is what makes the difference, because once it has spread across the leaves it is hard to turn around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Pulling the most heavily coated leaves early removes inoculum and opens the canopy at the same time. The value is concentrated at first signs, since control gets difficult once coverage and yellowing set in.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A biofungicide, a spray based on helpful microbes, can hold it back if you start at the first spots and repeat as the label directs.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A labeled biofungicide suppresses rather than cures. Begin at first signs and repeat on the label interval, since no curative role is on offer once the leaves are coated.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sulfur is the standard organic spray for powdery mildew. Start it at the first signs and repeat as the label says. If the spring crop is nearly finished anyway, picking what is ready and pulling the plants is often the simpler move.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur suppresses powdery mildew when begun early and repeated per label. On a spring crop close to done, harvesting out and pulling the planting is frequently the more practical call than starting a spray program.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the main answer. Sugar Snap and Cascadia are snap varieties that carry wilt resistance, and resistant snap peas are easy to find.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Resistant snap peas are not hard to source, Sugar Snap and Cascadia among them. Several races of the fungus exist, and with no curative option and a soil population that lingers for years, variety choice still carries the program.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Shift the crop to fresh ground and let three to four years pass before peas come back, so they are not dropped straight into infested soil.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A three to four year rotation off infested ground is the second lever. The fungus persists in soil for years, so rotation manages exposure rather than clearing the bed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Work on the drainage where you grow peas. Better-drained ground is part of the standard advice for keeping this one down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Improve drainage before peas return to the bed, and treat it as a companion to the rotation above rather than a substitute for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull affected plants and throw them out rather than composting them. Nothing will cure a plant once it is infected, so removal is about keeping the fungus from building up. Try not to carry soil from an infested bed onto a clean one.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infected plants are not recoverable, and removing and destroying them limits further buildup. Avoiding the transfer of infested soil between beds keeps clean ground clean.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Sow into ground that drains well, or build a raised bed. A cold, low, wet corner of the garden is the hardest place to bring peas up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Site and drainage set the outcome here. Free-draining or raised ground shortens the spell in which cold, saturated soil holds ungerminated seed and slow seedlings exposed.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wait for the soil to warm and drain before you sow, and keep seed out of soggy ground. Be gentle with the roots as you plant. If a sowing has already rotted, sow again once the soil has dried and warmed.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soil warmth and moisture at sowing govern this one: hold off on waterlogged ground, avoid root injury at planting, and replant a failed stand only once conditions have improved, since rotted seed and collapsed seedlings offer nothing to rescue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give the bed a break. Plant peas somewhere else and let three to four years go by before they return, since growing them in one spot too often lets these organisms build up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A three to four year rotation is aimed particularly at Aphanomyces, which accumulates in beds cropped to peas too frequently and kills plants outright where infection is severe.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull any plants that have already rotted, and clear the old pea vines out of the bed after harvest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing affected plants in season and stripping crop debris after harvest limits further loss. The organisms are resident in the soil, so this supports prevention rather than standing in for it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Some pea varieties offer partial tolerance to root rot, worth asking about if this keeps happening in your garden. Treat it as extra help rather than a fix.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Partial root-rot tolerance exists in some varieties. It is a margin on top of drainage, sowing conditions and rotation, not a control in its own right.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Buy seed sold as certified disease-free, and skip saving your own off a crop that showed this. The fungus rides in the seed itself, so where your seed comes from is a big part of the outcome.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The complex is seed-borne, so certified clean seed closes the most direct route in. Seed saved off an infected crop carries the fungi straight into the next planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pull affected plants and throw them out rather than composting them, and clear every scrap of old pea debris from the bed after harvest. Infected tissue cannot be cured, so removal is what slows it down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Infected tissue is not recoverable. Taking out affected plants in season and stripping all pea residue after harvest cuts the debris-borne carryover that starts the next outbreak.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Once a bed has carried it, leave peas out of that ground for three to four years at the least before planting them there again.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A minimum three to four year break off that ground lets the debris-borne inoculum run down before peas return.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the top. Splashing water is what carries this fungus from leaf to leaf.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Overhead irrigation supplies the splash dispersal these fungi depend on. Base watering removes that route and keeps the canopy drier at the same time.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Stay out of the pea rows while the vines are wet. Brushing past wet plants splashes the fungus onto healthy growth.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Working among wet vines splashes and carries the fungus through the planting. This is a timing discipline, decided by when you handle the crop rather than by what you apply.
